channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Rail
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] A private cellular APN carried attackers into a Polish power plant — the same network model rail runs its trackside gear on
item.description: CERT.PL has published a detailed account of a previously undisclosed intrusion into Poland’s energy sector, and the path matters more to rail than the target does. The attackers first compromised an internet-facing FortiGate appliance serving as firewall and VPN concentrator at a wind farm. From there they scanned the carrier-managed private APN — the cellular network the operator used to reach remote sites — for VNC, HTTP, Modbus and S7 services, and found a WAGO PFC200 controller at a combined heat and power plant with a WAN-facing management interface secured only by default credentials. They enabled SSH on the device, tunnelled into the plant’s OT network, and stopped a steam turbine and the process water treatment system; several ICS devices were permanently bricked during the clean-up. The intrusion itself dates to 29 December 2025, and heat and electricity deliveries to the plant’s roughly 50,000 customers were not interrupted, so this is a disclosed past event rather than live activity. CERT.PL describes it as the first publicly documented case of an attacker using a private APN as a lateral-movement path between sites, and warns the underlying misconfiguration — a flat cellular bearer with no segmentation between customer devices — is common internationally. That is the part rail cannot treat as someone else’s problem. Carrier-managed private APNs are the standard way freight and passenger railroads and transit agencies connect trackside signal cabinets, level-crossing controllers, depot systems and rolling-stock telemetry back to a control centre, precisely because they are marketed as a closed, carrier-isolated network. Almost no operator has asked the carrier in writing what else shares that APN, whether it is segmented device-to-device, or what happens if one compromised cabinet can reach another. Reporting also links the wider campaign — roughly 30 other Polish energy sites — to Russia-linked activity, though this specific facility’s attribution rests on the CERT.PL report rather than a formal government statement. - CERT.PL energy-sector incident follow-up report — via SecurityWeek - Report published 10–11 Aug 2026 (intrusion 29 Dec 2025)

item.title: [High] A dozen-state PLC lockout campaign shows what an exposed wayside controller costs an operator
item.description: Since 27–28 July, actors have reached internet-exposed Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers at water and wastewater utilities in at least 12 US states, changing device IP addresses and setting unauthorised passwords to lock operators out of monitoring and control. More than 30 Minnesota community systems were affected, a Georgia utility issued a boil-water advisory after a pump station failure, and New Jersey and Alabama joined the list in mid-August. Agencies assess the activity to Iranian-affiliated APT actors, publicly named as CyberAv3ngers, under joint advisory AA26-097A; no CVE was exploited — the actors used exposure plus default or weak credentials and the manufacturers’ own PLC programming software. No rail operator has been named in this campaign. What transfers directly is the equipment class and the technique: MicroLogix and similarly general-purpose PLC families run drawbridge and lock control, tunnel ventilation, station and depot pumping, and points heating on many railroads, and the same ‘exposed and left on default credentials’ failure mode applies regardless of which sector owns the device. - AA26-097A (FBI/CISA/NSA/EPA/DOE/USCYBERCOM/Treasury) and state disclosures — via SecurityWeek, NPR, TechCrunch - Campaign began late Jul 2026; New Jersey and Alabama confirmations 12–14 Aug 2026; AA26-097A updated 22 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s Gunra advisory describes the access pattern that would take down a railroad’s supporting systems, not its signalling
item.description: CISA and international partners issued a joint #StopRansomware advisory (AA26-222A) on Gunra, a Conti-derived ransomware-as-a-service operation running double-extortion campaigns against government and critical-infrastructure victims, typically entering through unpatched internet-facing VPN gateways and exposed RDP; the advisory cites Fortinet flaws CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 among the paths used, and Gunra has been observed giving victims five to seven days to pay before publishing stolen data. No rail-sector victim has been named in this advisory. The relevance to rail is the shape of the intrusion Dragos separately confirmed across the wider industrial ransomware picture this quarter: entry through an internet-facing edge device, then encryption of the enterprise and virtualisation estate rather than any direct manipulation of a control system. In rail that estate typically carries dispatch support, passenger information, ticketing, crew rostering and maintenance management — none of it safety-critical individually, all of it required to run a normal timetable. - CISA/FBI joint advisory AA26-222A - Advisory published 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] North Carolina’s three port facilities went to manual processing after an IT breach — and the OT question is still open
item.description: An outside actor breached IT systems at the North Carolina State Ports Authority around 5 August, forcing Wilmington, Morehead City and the Charlotte inland terminal onto manual cargo processing; a spokesperson confirmed the breach but the authority has declined to say whether ransomware was involved. The incident was described as contained, with normal operating schedules resuming 6–7 August, though some processing reportedly remains manual. No confirmation exists either way on whether any crane, gate or terminal-operating-system technology was reached — officials have not said it was compromised, but they have not ruled it out either. Ports are freight rail’s handoff point: container and bulk terminals commonly interchange directly with on-dock or near-dock rail, so a multi-day disruption at any port’s gate and yard systems ripples into intermodal train scheduling and railcar dwell even when the railroad’s own systems are untouched and the incident never appears in a railroad’s own reporting. - North Carolina State Ports Authority statement — via The Record - Intrusion 5 Aug 2026; publicly reported 6 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Siemens patches Ruggedcom APE1808, the substation platform that also runs rail wayside and trackside networking
item.description: Siemens’ August ProductCERT release includes two fixes for Ruggedcom APE1808, an application-hosting platform built into substation and field-network equipment: CVE-2026-23573, a cross-site scripting flaw, and CVE-2026-59839, a path-traversal issue inherited from bundled Fortinet components, rated CVSS 6.1 and 5.5. Siemens markets APE1808 explicitly for transportation substations as well as energy substations, and railroads use the same class of ruggedised, DIN-rail-mounted networking gear to carry signalling, SCADA and telemetry traffic between trackside cabinets, level crossings and control centres. Neither flaw is known to be exploited, but both require an update plus separate attention to the underlying Fortinet guidance, since the path-traversal issue rides in through third-party components rather than Siemens’ own code. - Siemens ProductCERT advisory — via CISA ICS advisories - Published as part of the Aug 2026 ICS Patch Tuesday, 11–13 Aug

item.title: [Medium] A malformed BACnet packet can freeze Siemens Desigo building controllers used in stations and depots
item.description: Siemens patched CVE-2026-59693 (CVSS 4.3) in Desigo DXR2 and PXC3/4/5/7 room and building automation controllers: a specially crafted BACnet packet causes the controller to stop responding until it is manually reset, a denial-of-service rather than a code-execution flaw. Desigo hardware runs heating, ventilation, lighting and access-adjacent building systems in commercial and institutional buildings, including station concourses, depots and administrative buildings on many railroads and transit agencies. A frozen building controller is not itself a safety event, but stations that lose HVAC or lighting control during a service disruption compound whatever else is going wrong, and depot buildings with frozen environmental controls can affect maintenance operations. Firmware updates are available from Siemens. - Siemens ProductCERT / CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-225-08 - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Critical Johnson Controls C-CURE 9000 and victor flaws could hand an attacker a station’s access-control system
item.description: Johnson Controls updated its advisory (Update A, 11 August) for C-CURE 9000 and victor, its physical access-control and video platforms, covering three vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-21655 and CVE-2026-21653, two critical unauthenticated deserialization flaws, and CVE-2026-34496, a high-severity issue, with CVSS scores up to 9.6. A network-adjacent attacker who reaches the server can execute code and take over the system without authenticating. C-CURE and victor are widely deployed for station, depot and administrative-building access control and CCTV across transit agencies and railroads, meaning a successful exploit would give an attacker control of door locking, badge access and camera systems at the facilities running it — a genuine physical-security consequence rather than a purely IT one. - Johnson Controls advisory; CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-204-01 (Update A) - Updated 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] An actively exploited Cisco firewall flaw hit CISA’s KEV list with a three-day deadline — and ASA/FTD sit at a lot of rail perimeters
item.description: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-20349, a heap-inspection denial-of-service flaw in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and FTD software, rated CVSS 8.6. It is being actively exploited to crash appliances, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 August with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Hotfixes cover all affected 9.x, 7.x and 10.x branches; there is no workaround. ASA and FTD are commonly deployed as the boundary device between corporate networks and operational technology, including the appliance that carries vendor and engineering remote access into signalling and depot systems on many railroads. An appliance an attacker can force to reload on demand is not a control anyone can rely on during an incident. - Cisco security advisory; CISA KEV catalogue — via BleepingComputer - Patched and KEV-listed 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA released 15 ICS advisories in a single day — several touch equipment classes rail also runs
item.description: CISA published 15 industrial control system advisories on 13 August alone, spanning AVEVA, Hitachi Energy, ANDRITZ, Siemens and Johnson Controls, with several flagged for the energy sector. Beyond the Ruggedcom, Desigo and C-CURE items covered separately, the batch includes AVEVA Enterprise SCADA / HMI (CVE-2025-7639, CVSS 7.1, untrusted deserialization exploitable by an authenticated operator-level user, patched), Hitachi Energy APM Edge transformer-monitoring appliances (CVE-2026-43284 and CVE-2026-43500, CVSS 8.8 and 7.8, with patch status unresolved and sources conflicting on firmware availability), and the Siemens License Server (CVE-2026-69109 and CVE-2026-69108, roughly CVSS 7.5, fixed). None of the 15 is known to be exploited. The volume itself is the point: a single-day batch this size is routine for August Patch Tuesday, but it means every OT security team, including rail infrastructure and rolling-stock groups, is triaging more than a dozen vendor advisories against their own asset inventory in the same week. - CISA ICS advisories, 13 Aug 2026 — via WaterISAC - 15 advisories published in one day, 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Forescout counted 4,407 exposed Rockwell controllers worldwide — the same discontinued families rail depots still run
item.description: Forescout Vedere Labs scanned for internet-reachable Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley controllers and found 4,407 worldwide, 2,844 of them in the United States, dominated by discontinued legacy MicroLogix 1400 and 1100 units — the same product family targeted in the ongoing water-sector campaign, and 22 of the exposed devices Forescout found sit in cities already hit by that campaign. Forescout found the intruders reconfiguring devices directly, using vendor engineering software rather than exploiting a new vulnerability. Rail infrastructure and yard-equipment teams commonly run the same discontinued MicroLogix and CompactLogix families for depot power monitoring and points and signal auxiliary equipment, kept in service well past their support window because replacement means a possession. The finding is not that rail has been targeted; it is that the same reachable, out-of-support controller class this campaign is walking through is common wherever legacy Rockwell gear was never pulled off the internet. - Forescout Vedere Labs research — via The Hacker News, CyberScoop - Published 6 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Dragos’s Q2 count puts rail at just 3 ransomware incidents — and confirms why: attacks stop at IT, not the signalling system
item.description: Dragos’s Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis recorded 1,140 incidents against industrial organisations worldwide, up 12% on Q1. Manufacturing absorbed 747 of them, roughly two-thirds; transportation and logistics accounted for 95 in total, split across maritime (8), aviation (6) and rail (3). No rail victim was named, and Dragos observed no case across any sector this quarter where ransomware operators reached Stage 2 of the ICS Cyber Kill Chain or directly manipulated a control system — disruption cascaded from IT encryption instead, most often through virtualisation and enterprise infrastructure. Rail’s low count this quarter is genuinely thin data rather than genuine immunity: three incidents worldwide is not a trend, and the pattern Dragos documents elsewhere — ticketing, dispatch support and passenger information going down through the same enterprise-IT path — is exactly the failure mode a railroad or transit agency should plan around even without a rail-specific incident to point to. - Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis - Published 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [Low] Congress moves to fund water-utility cybersecurity after the PLC campaign — rail has no equivalent bill
item.description: Senators Klobuchar and Schiff introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act on 13 August, responding directly to the multi-state PLC campaign against water utilities: it would give EPA authority to require cybersecurity assessments, fund $300 million a year in state revolving loan funds, and add a cyber-risk requirement to resilience planning for large water systems. New York separately awarded $9 million in SECURE grants to 153 drinking-water and wastewater systems, up to $50,000 for assessments and $100,000 for improvements per system. Rail has no comparable legislative funding mechanism on the table this window. The industry operates under existing TSA rail cybersecurity requirements that impose reporting and mitigation obligations, but nothing resembling a dedicated federal or state grant programme sized for smaller freight short lines and transit agencies the way this bill targets small water utilities. Whether Congress extends the same model to rail, given the parallel exposure argument — legacy PLCs and general-purpose controllers reachable from the internet at resource-constrained operators — is worth watching rather than assuming. - Office of Sen. Klobuchar statement - Bill introduced 13 Aug 2026
